title: The Trait You Can't Stand in Other People

reels.hook: Whose behaviour took up more of your week than it deserved?
reels.hook_b: Who got under your skin this week?
cards: Whose behaviour took up more of your week than it deserved?
Some of it is a mirror.
Ask quietly: is there a version of this in me?
If there is, call it a mistake. Not a verdict.
Send this to someone who'll admit theirs.
reels.visual: V3 still of a reflection in a dark window (tag window-reflection), else V1 + grain.
reels.caption:
In two lab studies, people told they had a feared trait saw more of it in a stranger, and projecting it seemed to help them deny it in themselves.

That doesn't make every irritation a mirror. It makes it worth a question.

What trait in other people gets to you most?

Evidence: Schimel, Greenberg & Martens (2003). Jung's "shadow" is an interpretive idea, not a tested therapy. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: One word: the trait in other people you can't stand.

reels.caption:
Eighteen centuries before Jung wrote about projection, Marcus Aurelius gave himself an instruction: when someone's fault offends you, turn to yourself and ask where you go wrong in a similar way.

Who's been your teacher this week, without meaning to be?

Source: Meditations 10.30, tr. George Long. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.

notes: Jung's shadow is an interpretive idea, not a tested therapy. But lab psychology has found something close to one part of it: in a 2003 study, people told they had a feared trait saw more of it in a stranger. This week's essay holds both, honestly.
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 10.30: "When thou art offended at any man's fault, forthwith turn to thyself." Eighteen centuries before anyone said "projection".
Not every irritation is a mirror. Some people are just rude. The useful question isn't "what's wrong with them?" It's "why is this taking up so much room in me?"
